title: Time: hours and minutes, the 24-hour clock and finish times
blurb: Convert between hours and minutes, use the 24-hour clock, and work out infusion durations and finish times, including across midnight.
question: An infusion of 1000 mL is started at 2130 and runs at 125 mL per hour. At what time will it finish?

teach.body: Time works in sixties: 1 hour = 60 minutes. The 24-hour clock writes times as four digits from 0000 to 2359, so 7.45 pm is 1945 and 12.15 am is 0015. Plain English: a decimal hour is a fraction of 60 minutes, so 0.5 h is 30 minutes and 0.25 h is 15 minutes, not 25. Infusion charts, prescription charts and fluid balance charts all use the 24-hour clock.

head: Hours
Minutes
teach.caption: Hours to minutes: x 60. Minutes to hours: ÷ 60.

teach.h: Worked example: surgical ward, night shift
items: Staff nurse Kofi Mensah starts 1000 mL at 125 mL per hour at 2130.
Add: 2130 + 8 hours = 2930, which is past midnight.
Sense check: 2130 to midnight is 2.5 hours; another 5.5 hours takes it to 0530.

teach.text: The classic error is reading the digits after the point as minutes: 6.25 hours is 6 hours 15 minutes, not 6 hours 25 minutes. Likewise you cannot subtract clock times as ordinary numbers: 1530 - 0845 is not 685 minutes. Work in hours and minutes, or convert both times to minutes first.

teach.body: Count forward in steps: from 0845 to 0900 is 15 minutes, 0900 to 1500 is 6 hours, 1500 to 1530 is 30 minutes: total 6 hours 45 minutes, or 405 minutes. Across midnight, count to 2400 first, then on from 0000.

items: 1 hour = 60 minutes: x 60 for minutes, ÷ 60 for hours.
Decimals of an hour are fractions of 60: 0.25 h = 15 min.
Past 2400, subtract 2400 and it is the next day.
Count durations forward in steps; do not subtract clock times as numbers.

summary: You can now convert between hours and minutes without the decimal-minutes trap, write times in the 24-hour clock, and work out durations and infusion finish times, including those that run past midnight.

whyNot.0: Read 1.25 h as 1 hour 25 minutes; 0.25 h is 15 minutes.
whyNot.1: Multiplied by 100; hours to minutes is x 60.
whyNot.3: Multiplied by 6; hours to minutes is x 60.

A.q: An infusion starts at 1415 and runs for 6 hours. At what time does it finish? Give the time in the 24-hour clock as four digits.

whyNot.0: Gave the 12-hour clock figure; 8.15 pm is 2015.
whyNot.3: Added 7 hours; the infusion runs for 6.

A.q: A dose is due at 7.45 pm. How is this written in the 24-hour clock?
A.why: Afternoon and evening times add 12 to the hour: 7.45 pm = 1945.

whyNot.2: Added 10 hours; pm times add 12 hours.
whyNot.3: Added 13 hours; pm times add 12 hours.

B.q: An infusion runs from 0845 to 1530 on the same day. For how many minutes does it run?
B.why: 0845 to 1445 = 6 hours; 1445 to 1530 = 45 minutes. 6 x 60 + 45 = 405 minutes.

whyNot.0: Subtracted the clock times as ordinary numbers (1530 - 845).
whyNot.1: Counted 7 hours 25 minutes; it is 6 hours 45 minutes.
whyNot.2: Counted 5 hours 45 minutes; 0845 to 1445 is already 6 hours.

B.q: An infusion has run for 200 minutes. How many hours is this? Write your answer to two decimal places.
B.why: 200 ÷ 60 = 3.333..., which is 3.33 hours to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: Wrote 3 hours 20 minutes as 3.2; 20 minutes is 0.33 h.
whyNot.2: Rounded to one decimal place; the question asks for two.
whyNot.3: Divided by 100; minutes to hours is ÷ 60.

B.q: 1000 mL is set to run at 125 mL per hour, starting at 2200. At what time will it finish? Give the time in the 24-hour clock as four digits.

whyNot.1: Added 8 hours without subtracting 2400 for the new day.
whyNot.2: This is 6 pm; the infusion ends at 6 am the next morning, which is 0600.

C.q: 500 mL is set to run at 80 mL per hour, starting at 0930. At what time will it finish? Give the time in the 24-hour clock as four digits.

whyNot.0: Read 6.25 hours as 6 hours 25 minutes; 0.25 h is 15 minutes.
whyNot.3: Gave the 12-hour clock figure; 3.45 pm is 1545.

C.q: A medicine is given every 8 hours. The first dose is given at 2200. At what time is the third dose due? Give the time in the 24-hour clock as four digits.
C.why: Doses at 2200, 0600 and 1400: the third dose is at 1400.

whyNot.3: This is when the fourth dose is due, 24 hours after the first.

C.q: 0.75 L is set to run at 100 mL per hour. How many minutes will it take?

reteach.title: Clock face, not calculator
reteach.question: Why is 2.5 hours not the same as 2 hours 50 minutes?

blocks.body: A calculator gives decimals of an hour; the clock counts in 60 minutes. Change the decimal part to minutes by multiplying by 60: 0.5 x 60 = 30, 0.25 x 60 = 15, 0.2 x 60 = 12. Only then add to the start time.

blocks.text: If the minutes in your finish time come to 60 or more, carry an hour: 1450 + 20 min is 1510, not 1470.

explain.body: From midnight to 0059 the hour digits are 00. Afternoon times add 12.

test.q: How is a quarter past midnight written in the 24-hour clock?
test.why: Midnight is 0000, so 15 minutes later is 0015.

whyNot.0: The 24-hour clock runs to 2359, then restarts at 0000.
whyNot.1: This is a quarter past midday.
whyNot.2: This is a quarter past one in the morning.

whyNot.0: Read 0.4 h as 40 minutes; multiply by 60.
whyNot.2: Multiplied by 10; hours to minutes is x 60.
whyNot.3: Multiplied by 6; hours to minutes is x 60.

explain.body: Divide the minutes by 60 and add to the whole hours. 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75.

test.q: Write 2 hours 45 minutes in hours. Write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: Wrote the minutes after the point; 45 minutes is 0.75 h.
whyNot.1: Rounded to one decimal place; the question asks for two.
whyNot.2: This is the total in minutes, labelled as hours.

explain.body: Add the duration, then subtract 2400 if the result passes 2400.

test.q: An infusion starts at 1930 and runs for 10 hours. At what time does it finish? Give the time in the 24-hour clock as four digits.

whyNot.1: Did not subtract 2400 for the new day.
whyNot.3: Gave the time 2 hours earlier on the same day.
